question: Why can averaging resampled minimum-norm linear interpolators remove the catastrophic risk spike that remains in any single sketched interpolator?

key_findings.claim: Multiplier-bootstrap bagging unifies classical bootstrap, Bernoulli subsampling, and other nonnegative row-weight sketches as ensembles of minimum-norm least-squares estimators.
key_findings.evidence: Each bootstrap replicate is a diagonal sketch of the design, its minimum-norm solution is computed, and replicate coefficients are averaged. The framework separates the effect of reducing effective sample size from the additional effect of averaging independent sketches.

key_findings.claim: Sketching alone shifts the interpolation threshold but retains an unbounded variance spike, whereas infinite bagging yields bounded limiting prediction risk.
key_findings.evidence: In the proportional regime d/n tending to gamma, exact random-matrix risk formulas show that a single sketch behaves like a changed aspect ratio and diverges near its new threshold. Cross-replicate covariance cancels the unstable idiosyncratic variance when estimators are averaged.

key_findings.claim: Bernoulli and classical multiplier bootstraps have the same limiting bagged risk under the stated moment conditions, while Bernoulli sketching is computationally attractive.
key_findings.evidence: The bagged limit depends on the retained mass rather than the full multiplier distribution, and simulations match the equivalence. Runtime measurements show that simple Bernoulli row selection is cheaper than multinomial/classical or orthogonal alternatives in the tested setup.

key_findings.claim: Bagging acts as an implicit regularizer: in the isotropic setting its ensemble solution is asymptotically equivalent to a suitably regularized full-sample estimator.
key_findings.evidence: Coefficient and risk comparisons derive an explicit regularization correspondence and simulations show shrinking norm differences from the matched ridge estimator. Extensions cover correlated features and deterministic/random signals.

method.core_idea: Use high-dimensional random-matrix asymptotics to decompose the generalization effect of resampling into threshold-shifting sketching and variance-reducing averaging.
method.mechanism: Rows receive independent nonnegative multiplier weights; each weighted design yields a minimum-norm interpolator and many replicas are averaged. Bias, variance, and cross-replica covariance are derived as n and d grow proportionally for isotropic and correlated features, then compared with matched ridge regularization and Monte Carlo simulations.
assumptions: Linear random-design regression with squared loss represents the instability mechanism of interest.
Sample size and feature dimension grow proportionally with limiting spectral distributions and bounded moments.
Bootstrap multipliers satisfy independence/nonnegativity and moment conditions.
The number of ensemble members is sufficiently large for the infinite-bagging approximation when applying the conclusions.

techniques.role: Represents multiple resampling schemes as diagonal design weights.
Provides the unstable base learner in the overparameterized regime.
Separates individual and cross-ensemble risk contributions.
Derives exact asymptotic risk around interpolation thresholds.
Interprets ensemble stabilization as explicit regularization.

evaluations.setting: Isotropic Gaussian random-design linear regression across aspect ratios and bootstrap retention rates.
evaluations.metric: Out-of-sample prediction risk, bias, and variance.
evaluations.result: Single sketches move but retain the double-descent divergence; bagged estimators remain bounded and can beat the full-sample min-norm solution over substantial regimes.
evaluations.baseline: Full-sample minimum-norm and individual sketched interpolators.

evaluations.setting: Bernoulli, classical multinomial, jackknife, and orthogonal sketches/ensembles.
evaluations.result: Several multiplier laws share the same infinite-bagging limit, while Bernoulli sampling is especially simple and fast in the reported computation.

evaluations.setting: Correlated features plus deterministic and random signal alignments.
evaluations.metric: Theoretical and simulated test risk under population spectral distributions.
evaluations.result: The bounded-risk and regularization interpretations extend with more complex fixed-point formulas, and simulations track the asymptotic curves.
evaluations.baseline: Isotropic formulas and full-sample min-norm/ridge estimators.

limitations: The analysis is asymptotic linear regression with squared loss, not nonlinear ensemble training.
Infinite-ensemble formulas omit the finite-B Monte Carlo variance and wall-clock cost practitioners face.
Results depend on random-design and spectral-limit conditions and do not cover adversarial/heavy-tailed designs broadly.
Model selection for retention probability or matched regularization is not solved from finite data.
failure_modes: Too aggressive subsampling can increase bias more than averaging reduces variance.
A small ensemble can retain substantial instability near the shifted threshold.
Strongly aligned signal and covariance spectra can invalidate intuition from isotropic risk curves.
Parallel bagging can be more expensive than directly fitting a well-tuned ridge model.
reusable_insights: Analyze randomized ensembles in two stages: what one randomization changes and what cross-member averaging cancels.
Interpolation thresholds are properties of effective aspect ratio, so resampling can move rather than remove the risk spike.
An ensemble may be understood through an equivalent deterministic regularizer, enabling cheaper approximations.
open_questions: What finite-ensemble size is sufficient to control risk near interpolation for realistic designs?
Do analogous implicit-regularization formulas hold for bagged kernel, tree, or neural interpolators?
Can retention probability be selected without a validation split while preserving the stability guarantee?

competitive_landscape.title: Reconciling modern machine learning practice and the bias-variance trade-off
competitive_landscape.relationship: Develops a high-dimensional view of interpolation and double descent in simple regression models.
competitive_landscape.difference: It characterizes the base interpolation phenomenon; this paper asks how sketching and bootstrap averaging transform its risk curve and supplies exact ensemble limits.

competitive_landscape.title: Benign Overfitting in Linear Regression
competitive_landscape.relationship: Characterizes when a minimum-norm interpolating linear predictor can generalize despite fitting noise.
competitive_landscape.difference: It derives conditions for a single interpolator's benign behavior; this paper stabilizes otherwise divergent regimes by resampling and averaging and compares that effect with ridge.

competitive_landscape.title: Deep Double Descent: Where Bigger Models and More Data Hurt
competitive_landscape.relationship: Documents interpolation-associated risk peaks empirically in deep learning and across model/data scale.
competitive_landscape.difference: It is primarily empirical and descriptive; the ensemble-linear paper gives a tractable mechanism showing why averaging can remove the variance divergence in a proportional linear model.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Multiplier-bootstrap bagging produces a bounded high-dimensional risk where every constituent sketched interpolator can diverge, and is equivalent to explicit regularization.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Closed-form asymptotic bias/variance results, multiplier-law equivalences, correlated-design extensions, and simulations jointly support the claim.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The clean separation of sketching from averaging is a strong theoretical contribution; translation to finite nonlinear ensembles is open rather than established.

reviewer_notes: Read the main 30 pages and proof structure across the 82-page extraction. Comparator records for interpolation, benign overfitting, and double descent were checked at primary arXiv pages on 2026-08-23.
